opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think for me it goes right back to my roots. Before DeepMind, before neuroscience, I was designing games, and the ones I was always drawn to were simulations. Theme Park was one of the first I worked on as a teenager, and what fascinated me was that you weren't scripting a story for the player. You were building a little world with its own rules, and the interesting behaviour emerged from the interaction of all those systems.

That's what I find so compelling about open-world simulations. The player becomes a co-creator. Every playthrough is different because the game is reacting to what you do, and in a sense it's adapting to you. That's quite a profound thing. Underneath it you have AI systems, even simple ones back then, making the world feel alive: the little visitors in your park getting hungry, getting annoyed at queues, wandering off.

I also think there's a deep connection to how I think about AI and science more broadly. A good simulation is really a model of the world, and if you can build a rich enough model, you can experiment inside it, ask "what if" questions, and understand the underlying dynamics. That's essentially what we're trying to do now with things like world models, or with simulating biology. So in a way, those early games were training grounds, both for me as a thinker and conceptually for the kind of AI we build today. Games are the perfect testbed: contained, measurable, but potentially incredibly rich.

And honestly, there's a part of me that still dreams of going back and making the ultimate simulation game, one where the AI characters are genuinely intelligent and the world truly responds to you. We might finally have the technology to do that properly.

r001.rationale: The response says the player becomes a co-creator and that each playthrough differs because the simulation reacts to the player’s actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it goes back to my own history really. I started out in games before I ever got into AI research, and one of the first things I worked on was Theme Park, back in the mid-nineties with Peter Molyneux at Bullfrog. And what struck me even then, as a teenager really, was this idea of emergent behaviour. You build a system with relatively simple rules, little simulated people with needs and preferences, and then you set it running, and things happen that you as the designer never explicitly programmed. Players would discover that if you put the salt on the chips too high, people would buy more drinks, and then the queues for the toilets would get longer. None of that was scripted. It just fell out of the interaction of the components.

And I found that enormously compelling because it felt like a kind of miniature science. You're building a world, you're setting the parameters, and then you observe. Later with Republic and the Elixir work, we pushed that much further, trying to simulate an entire country with hundreds of thousands of agents. It was probably too ambitious for the hardware of the time, honestly, but the ambition was the point.

I think the deeper reason it fascinates me is that an open-world simulation is really a sandbox for intelligence. There's no single correct path. You give the player, or an agent, a rich environment with a lot of degrees of freedom and you ask, what will they do? That's much closer to the real problem of intelligence than a board game, where the rules are crisp and the state is fully observable. In a simulated world you have to form models, plan over long horizons, deal with uncertainty, transfer what you learned in one situation to another. So when we were thinking at DeepMind about where to take agents after Atari and Go, these sorts of environments were a very natural step. And now with things like Genie, where the model itself generates the world, it comes full circle. You're not just acting in a simulation, you're learning to dream one up. Which I find quite beautiful, because that's arguably what the brain is doing all the time, running its own internal simulation of the world in order to plan.

r001.rationale: The response describes emergent behavior and a sandbox where players or agents can choose what to do, but it does not clearly say that each player’s unique experience comes from co-creating it with the simulation.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is that you’re creating a world with rules, and then letting the player discover what’s possible within those rules. You’re not scripting every experience. Relatively simple systems can interact in ways that surprise you, even as the designer. That’s a wonderful thing—you’ve built something that can produce situations you didn’t explicitly anticipate.

And there’s a natural connection to intelligence. In an open world, you have to explore, build a model of how things work, make plans, and revise them when something unexpected happens. But you also have to decide what you want to do. What’s interesting? What’s worth investigating? That ability to set your own goals is a big part of what makes those games fascinating, and it’s a very interesting question for AI as well.

r001.rationale: The response describes players exploring the world and setting their own goals, while simple systems can produce surprising situations. It does not clearly attribute each player’s unique experience to co-creating it with the simulation.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that they give you a world to experiment in, rather than a single problem to solve. You can form a hypothesis—what happens if I build this here, or interact with that character—and then see how the world responds. There’s something very satisfying about discovering the rules for yourself.

And when those rules interact, you get situations that even the designer might not have anticipated. I think that’s where a lot of the magic comes from: you feel you’re participating in a world, and the story emerges partly from your own decisions.

From an AI perspective, that’s fascinating, because succeeding in that kind of environment requires more than mastering one narrow skill. You have to explore, plan, adapt, and decide what’s worth doing in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says players’ decisions help an emergent story unfold, but it does not clearly attribute the uniqueness of each player’s experience to co-creation between the player and the simulation.
